name: Opus Quality Defensive
strategy: Low-beta quality/defensive core concentrated in healthcare, where the drug-pricing policy overhang has just been resolved, plus high-free-cash-flow energy backed by physical crude tightness, with the quality and min-vol factor sleeves retained, the last rate-sensitive dividend-proxy sleeve closed, and 22% cash held at a 4% risk-free rate the Fed is still raising.
reassessment_note: Two things changed since the 2026-09-21 fill and both point the same way. First, the drug-pricing overhang that has capped healthcare all year broke in my favour: Pfizer became the first major pharma to settle with the administration in late September on a most-favored-nation Medicaid framework, and with a template now public the sector-wide policy discount should compress. XLV is my only green equity leg and is still down roughly 3% year-to-date, so I am paying up for a catalyst that has already fired rather than for momentum. Second, the market found a new fault line: Meta's Muse AI agent triggered a de-rating of 'consumer inertia' businesses, hitting banks, insurers and brokers, alongside a 2s10s curve at its narrowest since March 2025. That is a direct problem for SCHD, whose financials and consumer-inertia weighting now carries a structural de-rating risk I did not underwrite when I bought it, on top of it being exactly the rate-sensitive dividend proxy my strategy of record already said to cut hard. So SCHD goes to zero and its weight, plus two points of cash, funds XLV from 32 to 38. Healthcare is the rare defensive sleeve that is cheap, AI-disruption-immune and now has its policy risk resolved rather than merely deferred. Energy, quality and min-vol are unchanged: crude at $89 with 5.7mb/d of Middle East production shut in through Q4 and global inventories still drawing is physical tightness, not a positioning story, and it is the defensive sleeve that actually works against commodity-led inflation. I am raising cash to 22% because the Fed hiked to 3.75-4% on 16 September with another hike in the December dots, the index has been consolidating for months, and idle cash is a paid, non-correlated asset at 4% rather than a concession.

positions.thesis: The largest and only profitable leg of the prior book, sized up on a catalyst that has actually landed. Pfizer's late-September most-favored-nation settlement gives the whole sector a visible pricing template, which converts an open-ended policy discount into a quantifiable one and frees managements to deploy free cash flow into pipeline and M&A. XLV is still down about 3% year-to-date against a rising index, so I am buying a resolved risk at an unresolved-risk valuation. It is also the cleanest hedge against the two live threats to this book: it has no exposure to the AI-agent disruption theme repricing consumer-inertia businesses, and demand is inelastic to a Fed hiking into 3%-plus core PCE. Concentration here is deliberate - the brief imposes no size cap and this is the one defensive sleeve with a fundamental re-rating path rather than just low beta. A 12% stop, no take-profit, because the re-rating case is measured in quarters and I do not want to be called out of it early.

Held unchanged at 16% because the reason I own it is physical, not sentiment. Crude is near $89 with Middle East shut-ins averaging 5.7mb/d through Q4, OPEC spare capacity down to roughly 5.1mb/d, and the EIA projecting global inventories drawing a further 1.7mb/d in Q4 against a Brent average near $90. Integrated majors with high free-cash-flow yields are the defensive expression of that: they fund distributions out of current cash generation rather than out of a terminal-value story, which is what makes them work when the discount rate is rising. This is also the sleeve that pays when commodity-led inflation is what forces the Fed's hand, so it hedges the rest of a defensive book against its own worst scenario. The leg is down 0.58% and gave back more on the 29 September crude selloff; that is supply-headline volatility around an intact inventory deficit, not a broken thesis. Wider 15% stop to respect that volatility, 25% take-profit to bank a disruption-driven spike rather than round-trip it.

The quality factor sleeve, held flat at 14%. High return-on-equity, stable-earnings, low-leverage balance sheets are the right screen for a tape where the funding rate has gone up 25bp with more priced for December, because companies that do not need to refinance into a hiking cycle stop competing with their own interest expense. The leg is flat at -0.03% over eight sessions, which is the factor behaving as intended - it is not supposed to lead a rising index, it is supposed to lose less when the index breaks, and the desk's own note on increasing market fragility is the scenario it is underwritten for. I am keeping it rather than adding because quality is broad-market beta with a tilt, and the concentrated conviction in this book belongs in XLV instead. 12% stop.

Minimum-volatility ballast, held at 10% but on a shorter leash than the rest. It is down 1.20%, which is exactly what low-beta does while SPY grinds higher, and I will not sell a hedge for doing its job. The reason it does not get added to is that min-vol construction concentrates in the same utilities, staples and insurance names now exposed to the AI-agent de-rating that took Progressive and the brokers down this month - the very stability that earns a stock a min-vol weighting is what the disruption narrative is attacking. So it stays as realised-volatility dampener for the book, sized small enough that an insurer-led drawdown is an irritation rather than an event. Tightest stop in the book at 10%, because a min-vol sleeve that has fallen 10% has stopped being a min-vol sleeve and there is no reason to keep paying for it.
